author: duncathan
text:
From the libcst readme:

For parsing, LibCST ships with a native extension, so releases are distributed as binary wheels as well as the source code. If a binary wheel is not available for your system (Linux/Windows x86/x64 and Mac x64/arm are covered), you’ll need a recent Rust toolchain for installing.

author: barry-scott
text: Check their PyPI page and see is they have a wheel for 3.14 released

author: nedbat
text: You shouldn’t have to dig around and find wheels yourself. Your library installer (pip install or uv pip install) should do that for you. How did you create your Python environment? What does python -V show? Can you show the complete installation command you ran and all of its output?

author: zware
text:
When you install a package, you also install all of its direct dependencies.  In this case, PyYAML does not yet provide wheels for Python 3.15, and so you would need a C toolchain to build it.  On Windows, installing either of Visual Studio Community or Build Tools for Visual Studio should be sufficient.
As @nedbat said, you do not need to go searching for wheels for yourself, pip (or uv) will find them on PyPI for you, if they exist.
Your other option is to install Python 3.14 (pymanager install 3.14), for which PyYAML provides current wheels.

author: zware
text:
Nick:

python -v output


There’s a big difference between python -v (verbose mode, which prints imports) and python -V (display the version); Ned asked about the version, but the question was answered (close enough) by the win-amd64-cpython-315 tag in the output provided.



 Nick:

there is one in pyyaml-cp315. Can I somehow use that instead?


 you could try, but I personally wouldn’t trust it.  Much simpler to follow the link provided in the failure output to get the Microsoft C++ Build Tools and be able to build your own.  If you so insist, you would need to make use of the --no-dependencies flag to pip install.

author: duncathan
text: pyyaml_cp315-6.0.3-cp315-cp315t-musllinux_1_2_x86_64.whl appears to be a Linux wheel, not a Windows wheel. If you’re unwilling to install the tool chain to compile it yourself, it sounds like your best course of action is to just stick to Python 3.14 until this package gets an appropriate wheel for 3.15.

author: nedbat
text:
win_amd64 in the file name means it’s for Windows. musllinux in the file name means it’s for Linux.
You really shouldn’t try to find and download your own wheels. Pip will find you the right ones if they are available. 3.15 is still quite new, and some projects haven’t yet provided the needed wheels. I would recommend using 3.14 for now.
